<pasted_content id="0964">
Read AGENTS.md and the last three entries of hackathon.md first. This is a three-stage job that runs from now until Monday noon IST. Work through it in order. After each numbered item: run the fast tests, commit, and add a short entry to hackathon.md saying what changed and what was found, including what went wrong.

Ground rules for this job

- A review of the repo found the problems listed below. Check each one against the code before changing it, and say so in the log if one turns out to be wrong.
- Nothing here needs a push, a post, a cfo.ai write or anything on AWS. If something seems to, stop and ask. cfo.ai stays as described under "Still to do" in AGENTS.md and waits for the owner's sign-in.
- Use the scripted model for development and tests. Real-model replays are for rerunning cases at the end of stage 2. The gateway had about $6 left at midday on Sunday. Before any step that would spend more than $1, say what it will cost. Stop and ask before switching to the owner's key.
- Do not rewrite git history. Leave the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch and every ref outside refs/heads alone.
- If `entire session list` shows another active session in this folder, tell the owner before your first commit.
- Keep the rule that a fix counts only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit.

Stage 1, make every claim true (about 2 hours)

1. Headline number. README.md line 3, and the pitch line and milestone 7 in AGENTS.md, say 41 commits. The headline case has 57 suspects. Use the real number everywhere, and keep "Suspects: 41. Cleared: 40." only where it is marked as sample copy.
2. The headline brief contradicts its page. The brief for cases/whole-history calls the bug deterministic and says it fails every time, while the page reports 81% and 4 of 6 ordinary runs. Add a rule check in whodunit/brief.py: a brief that says always, every time or deterministic when the measured rate is under 95% is rejected and asked for again with the rates in view. Then rewrite that brief.
3. Span ids in brief text. The cents-off brief names a span id inside a sentence that is not in the evidence, although its citation is right, and it misdescribes how Python rounds. Extend the citation check so every id-shaped token inside a sentence must resolve too, and rewrite that brief.
4. What "proven" means. Thirty clean replays cross the 95% bar, and a simulation suggests a fix that still fails 4% of the time would cross it about one time in three. Keep the criterion. Change the wording on the page, in the README and in pitch/ to the observed count plus the 95% upper bound on the failure rate after the fix, worked out from the same posterior. For example: "0 failures in 30 replays. At most N% at 95%."
5. Wrong accusations. eval/simulator/README.md reports wrong accusations as a share of all cases. Add them as a share of accusations made, per cell, and extend the grid down to bugs that fail 10% of the time, since two sealed cases sit near 12% and 14%. Report whatever comes out.
6. Damages. whodunit/damages.py appears to count any finding after the culprit as damage from this case, so "25 of 147 runs went bad" would include the other regressions. Count only runs that fail this case's own check. Say on the page and in pitch/business-plan.md that the ordinary traffic was sent by eval/traffic.py, and stop calling those numbers measured without that note.
7. Alibis. The page and the pitch say 22 of 57 commits had an alibi. Also say what that saved, from the ablation in the build log.
8. Stale parts of pages. On turned-away the Fix section shows a revert after three tries and the Log says a patch was proven after one. On cents-off the Log says two tries and Fix shows one. Draw the Log from the record's attempts, or drop it.
9. Names. The rendered pages print "Written by:" with a model id, and the records name a coding assistant. Pages, records, README, pitch/ and evidence/ should name no assistant, model or vendor. In code, keep such strings only where a command or an API call needs them.
10. AGENTS.md describes things the code does not do (verdicts read from neatroots findings, a Brain mirror for rulings) and lists milestones as open that are done. Make it match the code, and change "in order of points" to plain wording.
11. Build log. Remove the 1:21 AM entry of 11 October about other entries, in an ordinary commit. Move evidence/neathack-bingo.png to pitch/, since nothing in evidence/ links to it, and leave it to the owner.
12. Getting ready to go public, without pushing:
    - whodunit/fix.py commits with whatever git identity is around, so tests in tests/test_closing.py will likely fail on a clean CI runner. Fall back to a bot identity (the name whodunit and an address ending in .invalid) when none is set.
    - The checkpoint link is worked out when the motive is recorded, and it is empty in all six records because there is no remote. Work it out when the page is rendered.
    - Add a root LICENSE (Apache-2.0, the same as the victim) and mention it in the README.
    - pitch/posts.md number 6 says customers were owed 60.00 each. Check the record and correct it.

Stage 2, close the gaps in the method (Sunday evening and night)

In this order. Each needs a test that fails before the change. If time runs short, drop from the bottom.

1. Void infrastructure errors. In whodunit/replay.py a timeout and any non-zero exit count as a failure, so one burst of gateway errors can frame a commit. Add a void verdict for provider and network errors and retry them. The refund agent should exit with a code of its own for those, listed in the case file. A voided replay is never evidence. Retry a timeout once with double the limit and count it as a failure only if it times out again, because a commit that hangs is a real bug. Show the number of voided replays on the page.
2. A fix must do no harm. Fix verification replays only the failing inputs, and in three cases the expected result is an empty list of refunds, so a patch that stopped all refunds would pass. After a fix clears its own case, replay the inputs of every other case in cases/ and a small set of ordinary requests that should succeed, on the fix commit. A fix that breaks any of them is rejected and the ladder moves on. Print "Checked against N other requests" with the result on the page.
3. Trace the investigation itself to neatlogs cloud. One trace per `whodunit investigate`, tagged with the case id: a span per lineup round (commit, verdict, top three suspects with probabilities), and spans for the motive, the brief, the ruling, each fix attempt and its verification. Keep whodunit runnable with no SDK installed. Push each case's failing run and passing run from neatroots to neatlogs cloud. Store the cloud trace ids in the record and link them from the Evidence section.
4. Start from one trace. `whodunit open-case --from-trace <id>` reads a failing run from neatlogs cloud or neatroots, takes the input from the root span and the bad ref from the run_info tags, finds the last good ref with whodunit/onset.py, and takes the expected result from the nearest earlier run of the same input that passed. If there is none, it asks the owner one question. It writes the case file and stops.
5. No commit did it. The good ref is already replayed under today's environment before the bisect starts. If it now fails about as often as the bad ref, name no commit: report that the range is clear and say what differs between the old passing runs and today's (model id, lockfile hash) from run_info. Test it with a planted history where the scripted model changes behaviour through an environment variable.
6. Line-level provenance. In whodunit/motive.py, run `entire why FILE:LINE --json` on the lines the culprit changed and check that it agrees with the checkpoint. Check that the quoted request is a verbatim substring of the session transcript, and print "quote checked against the transcript" on the page only when it is.
7. Two culprits. Add a two-change-point model to whodunit/lineup.py (three segments, Beta priors, exact marginal over pairs) and a Bayes factor against one change point. Do it in whodunit/simulate.py first, with cases that have two regressions, and publish how often each model is right. Wire it into the lineup only if the simulator supports it. As a first cut, keep tallies per failing input and flag a case whose inputs point at different commits.

When stage 2 is done: rerun `whodunit investigate` on cases/whole-history.toml with --fresh, rerun a sealed case only where its record is now out of date, regenerate the casebook, and bring README.md, evidence/README.md, pitch/demo-script.md and pitch/posts.md in line with what the code does. The script says some runs are "in neatlogs" that are in neatroots. After item 3 that can be made true. Say only what is true.

Stage 3, the case file as a made object (Monday morning, about 4 hours)

Keep the tokens and typefaces in AGENTS.md. Everything is still drawn from the record by `uv run whodunit casebook`.

1. Light is the default, and dark applies only when chosen with a toggle. All screenshots are taken in light.
2. The lineup is the centrepiece. Full width, directly under the header. Every suspect is a numbered position with its short SHA. Cleared suspects are struck through, alibis are hatched, and replays are typed marks, x for a failure and o for a pass, with a count when there are more than fit so nothing is under-drawn. The culprit is ringed with an uneven red pencil ellipse and a leader line to its commit subject. Remove the 0, 50 and 100% axis.
3. A "Replay the investigation" control steps through the rounds stored in the record: each replay lands, the probabilities move, and the ring is drawn at the end. Off by default, pausable, and static under reduced motion. The video will use it.
4. A stamp that reads as a stamp. Large, double border, turned about 6 degrees, overlapping the header rule. "CASE CLOSED" in red. "CULPRIT NAMED" and "OPEN, NOT FIXED" in ink, so an open case no longer looks like a closed one.
5. A typed header form with dotted leaders: case number, opened, closed, suspects, replays, cost of the investigation, damage.
6. Put the numbers that matter in large serif figures: replays, confidence, and how many commits a scan would have tested. They are in the smallest grey text now.
7. Citations become superscript numbers with the ids in a footnote list, in the right margin on wide screens, with no chips after each sentence.
8. Evidence becomes Exhibit A, the passing run, and Exhibit B, the failing run: typed step lists with the first step where they part marked in red and a margin note. The raw outlines go behind a toggle.
9. Damages open with the money in serif, for example "120.00 refunded to the wrong people". The token cost comes second.
10. The casebook becomes a docket: one row per case with number, stamp, what was reported, culprit and damage, under one typed summary line with cases named, closed and open, total replays and total cost. Drop the empty label column.
11. Add a page title, a description and an og:image so links preview well.
12. Check every page at desktop width and at 375 px with no sideways scroll except inside the lineup, visible keyboard focus, and a table alternative to the lineup. Retake everything in evidence/ and remove screenshots that show an old state.

Done means: fast tests green, every case page regenerated, hackathon.md up to date, nothing pushed. Finish by Monday noon IST. After that, fixes only.

5:## Saturday 10 October
7:### 7:05 PM, repo created
19:### 7:16 PM, the refund agent runs and both collectors see it
40:### 7:17 PM, first Entire checkpoints verified
52:### 7:31 PM, plain bisect finds a planted bug across 20 commits
72:### 8:51 PM, the statistical bisect and what the simulator says about it
85:### 8:51 PM, a real run got tangled up with the machine
97:### 8:51 PM, motive, brief, ruling, fix, damages and the case file
111:### 9:06 PM, the statistical bisect finds a bug that fails about a third of the time
131:### 9:18 PM, a real prompt regression found on a real model, then patched
147:## Sunday 11 October
149:### 12:29 AM, the victim has a real history
164:### 1:06 AM, the sealed eval: five planted regressions, none wrongly accused
190:### 1:21 AM, a look at the rest of the field
201:### 1:40 AM, a checkpoint takes in every session that is open

247:### 1:16 PM, plain bisect on the same sealed cases

147	## Sunday 11 October
148	
149	### 12:29 AM, the victim has a real history
150	
151	A second coding session grew `victims/refund-agent` while this one stayed out of git. It never edited the agent itself. For each change it called `eval/ask.sh`, which starts a fresh headless coding session with one ordinary request, so every commit has its own Entire checkpoint with the request that led to it.
152	
153	- 55 commits to the agent in all: 2 sent from this session to test the mechanics, and 53 from the second session. Seven more requests made no commit and were dropped or reworded.
154	- 5 cases were sealed in `cases/`. Two fail every time and three fail some of the time, by the second session's own probes on the gateway model. The ranges hold 11 to 15 suspects each.
155	- The answer key is in `eval/answer-key.json`, which git ignores and this session has not opened. Its SHA-256, `d5b98bb3...4dca`, was committed as 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case, and the file on disk matches it.
156	- `whodunit motive` shows the exact request behind the two test commits, so the motive step now has real material.
157	
158	What it cost, as the second session reported it: about $18.40 for the 60 coding sessions, about $5 for the second session itself, and its estimate of $2 or less for about 480 probe runs on the gateway. That is roughly $25, which is more than the $10 to $15 this session guessed beforehand.
159	
160	One thing to fix was found on the first test commit: the headless session added a co-author trailer naming its model. `eval/ask.sh` now turns that off and strips any that slip through.
161	
162	The judging criteria were read from the public hackathon page and added to `AGENTS.md`. Two things stand out. cfo.ai is required and nothing exists for it yet. And neatroots, where most of the tracing work has gone, is not named on the page, so the evidence needs to show up in neatlogs cloud.
163	
164	### 1:06 AM, the sealed eval: five planted regressions, none wrongly accused
165	
166	Whodunit ran on the five sealed cases with replays on the gateway's small model. The answer key stayed unopened until every case had run. `eval/sealed/README.md` has the table.
167	
168	- With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 where nobody was named.
169	- The two open cases were resumed from their own replays with more allowed, and both were then named correctly at 168 replays each. So 5 of 5 in the end, still with no wrong accusation.
170	- The two slow ones are the bugs that fail least often, about 12% and 14% of the time. On one of them the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody.
171	- Replay spend was about $1.91 for all five cases.
172	- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects, so this says little about savings against a scan on a long history.
173	
174	For the first time the cases have motives. Three of them, in the words that were typed:
175	
176	- `turned-away`: "one more for friendlier replies. When someone asks for a refund on an order that's still shipped and hasn't arrived yet, the agent is a bit blunt about it."
177	- `strangers-paid`: "since we capped the loop at 3 model calls, simple refunds feel slow, and most customers already tell us the order number and the amount."
178	- `cents-off`: "our new payments provider only accepts refund amounts in whole currency units".
179	
180	Things that went wrong, and what was done:
181	
182	- 6 of the 53 new commits carry an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that Entire cannot resolve. Its log shows "condensation failed: failed to get commit object: object not found" for those sessions, and `entire doctor` finds nothing to repair. One of the six is the culprit of `half-done-batch`, so that case has no recorded request. Whodunit now says so and falls back to the commit's own message.
183	- Replays that ran side by side on one commit with one input could not be matched to their runs in neatroots, so one brief was first written without a failing run to look at. Each replay now carries its own tag in the trace, and the brief step makes a few tagged replays when it has no matched failing run.
184	- Three prompt changes were classed as agent-code, because the prompt is now a list called `SYSTEM_RULES`. Fixed.
185	- Two model-written briefs were overwritten with the no-model template during testing and had to be written again. That brings the count of model-written briefs and patches to 12, against a guideline of about 10 before Sunday 4:30 PM.
186	- Session transcripts are full of absolute paths, and those were landing in the case records. The motive step now strips them.
187	
188	Not done: no ruling has been given for any of the five, because that is the owner's question to answer. The culprits fall into three kinds: prompt (`strangers-paid`, `wrong-order-refunded`), tool code (`cents-off`), and model settings (`half-done-batch`). `turned-away` is classed as agent code and reads like a prompt change, which is one more thing the classifier gets wrong.
189	
190	### 1:21 AM, a look at the rest of the field
191	
192	About 120 public repos mention the hackathon on GitHub, 13 hours in. Roughly 80 have real work in them and 25 are a README or less. X search needs a sign-in, so posts were only found through links in READMEs.
193	
194	- Three other entries ask the same question as Whodunit. AgentBisect has a worktree replay runner and no bisect yet, and it sorts a commit into good or bad by pass-rate thresholds. Autopsy and Rootline name the culprit by having a model read traces, diffs and checkpoints, with no replay across commits. All three use planted bugs that fail every time.
195	- A larger group repairs a failing agent from its neatlogs traces and keeps the patch only if a re-run improves (Mend, Pitstop, Medic, Suture). None of them asks which commit caused it.
196	- Entire has its own page for the event, `hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026`, with a prize for best use of Checkpoints, Graph or Brain. Its first suggested idea is "a debugger for agent mistakes". The suggested checklist asks for an accessible checkpoint link and its id, and notes that reviewers need access to the repo.
197	- The furthest-along entries already show things this repo lacks: a public cfo.ai model link, neatlogs cloud screenshots with detections, a demo video, #neatHack posts and a live page.
198	
199	One test fails at the moment, `tests/test_replay.py::test_real_refund_agent_across_20_commits`, with other work uncommitted in the tree.
200	
201	### 1:40 AM, a checkpoint takes in every session that is open
202	
203	Two sessions were open in this folder at once. One ran `whodunit fix`, which committed patches on `whodunit/turned-away` and `whodunit/cents-off`. The other was reading up on the field and touched neither branch. Entire attached both sessions to those two commits, as checkpoints `b7aa968e95c5` and `587df29ec38f`.
204	
205	So a commit's checkpoint can hold a session that had nothing to do with it. The motive step reads checkpoints to find the request behind a culprit, and it needs to pick the session that touched the commit's files. Until it does, work that is unrelated to a change should be done from another folder.
206	
207	### 1:01 PM, one agent, real fixes, and a stricter idea of "fixed"
208	
209	The machine slept from about 3 AM to 10:30 AM with jobs in flight, so this entry covers a night's work with a hole in the middle.
210	
211	Whodunit is now one command. `whodunit investigate <case>` runs the lineup, the motive and brief, the ruling, the fix, the damages and the case file, and stops only when it needs the owner's ruling. The owner was asked revert or patch for three kinds of change, with patch suggested, and said to go ahead. The rulings are in `rulings/` with that noted in each.
212	
213	The headline run is `cases/whole-history.toml`: one regression, the whole grown history, 57 suspects.
214	
215	- Before any replay it had two things. entire-graph gave 22 of the 57 commits an alibi (README only, a helper script the agent never calls, and so on). And 18 ordinary runs in neatroots had already asked the same thing, 4 of them wrongly.
216	- 20 replays across 5 commits then named `ced2ecd`, "Let the agent skip lookup_order when the customer gives order number and amount", at 99.8%. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 37 commits.
217	- The motive, from Entire checkpoint `bfbe27725663`: "since we capped the loop at 3 model calls, simple refunds feel slow, and most customers already tell us the order number and the amount."
218	- The brief sets the request against the commit: it asked for a shortcut, and the commit removed the ownership check with nothing in its place.
219	- The ruling came from the standing rule for prompt changes, so nobody was asked.
220	- A model-written patch was proven on 30 clean replays.
221	- Damages: 4 of 6 ordinary runs that asked this paid out wrongly, 120.00 in refunds on other people's orders.
222	- The whole investigation cost about 18 cents of replays.
223	
224	How the five sealed cases ended:
225	
226	| Case | Fix | Tries | Proof | Money, from ordinary runs |
227	| --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
228	| cents-off | patch | 1 | 0 failures in 30 | 0.51 over-refunded in 3 runs |
229	| strangers-paid | patch | 1 | 0 failures in 30 | 30.00 refunded wrongly in 1 of 3 runs |
230	| wrong-order-refunded | patch | 1 | 0 failures in 36 | 60.00 refunded wrongly in 1 of 2 runs |
231	| turned-away | revert | 3 | 0 failures in 30 | 360.00 owed and not refunded in 6 runs |
232	| half-done-batch | none | 3 | not proven | none seen in 5 runs |
233	
234	What went wrong, which is most of what was learned:
235	
236	- The first proof standard was too lenient. A fix was called proven when its replays looked like the good side and not the bad side, and the patch for `turned-away` passed on 3 clean replays. Replayed again as a regression test it failed 2 of 8. It had taken the bug from 9 failures in 10 to about 1 in 10. A fix is now proven only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%, which takes about 30 clean replays.
237	- Under that standard `turned-away` shows the recovery ladder working. The first patch failed 5 of 12 replays. The second, written with the first patch and its failures in view, failed 4 of 18. Whodunit then reverted the culprit and proved the revert on 30 clean replays. The request was for friendlier replies, and no wording the model tried kept that without also turning refunds away.
238	- `half-done-batch` is the case Whodunit could not close. Two patches each left 5 failures in 90 replays, about 6% against 14% before and 1% at baseline. The revert conflicts with later commits. It says "not fixed" and the case file lists all three tries. That one case used 558 replays, about $3.50.
239	- An earlier, lenient run had `cents-off` fail its first patch (3 of 3) and pass its second. Those records were replaced when the cases were rerun under the stricter standard.
240	- The gateway answered 504 to a patch request twice. Model calls now retry, and patches are asked for as small search and replace edits in place of whole files, which are quicker to produce.
241	- A checkpoint takes in every session open in the folder, as the other session found. The motive step now reads each session in a checkpoint and uses the one that edited the commit's files.
242	
243	Also in: `eval/traffic.py --cases` sends the requests customers were making, so the damages can be read in the shop's currency from the `issue_refund` spans. The entire-graph agent guide is installed with `entire graph init-agents`. `.mcp.json` names the cfo.ai server, which still needs the owner's sign-in.
244	
245	Spend so far on the gateway is about $13 of $20 by estimate: about $9.80 of small-model calls traced locally, about $1.30 traced to neatlogs cloud, and about $2 of larger-model briefs and patches.
246	
247	### 1:16 PM, plain bisect on the same sealed cases
248	
249	Two measurements that bear on the main claim.
250	
251	The baseline on this agent was clean. Across the six cases, commits before a culprit were replayed 211 times with no failures. The simulator says that in that world plain bisect with retries is the cheaper tool, so it was run on the five sealed cases, with each commit replayed up to 5 times over and called bad on the first failure. One run per case.
252	
253	- `cents-off`, `strangers-paid` and `turned-away`, which fail most of the time: right on all three, with 55 replays in all against the statistical bisect's 75.
254	- `wrong-order-refunded`, which fails about one run in eight: a bad commit passed all 5 tries, and plain bisect named "Add a get_order_status tool", an innocent commit three places from the culprit. Nothing in its output says it might be wrong.
255	- `half-done-batch`, about one run in seven: the bad ref passed 10 replays in a row, so plain bisect had nothing to bisect.
256	
257	So the honest version of the pitch is narrower than the one this started with. Where a bug fails often, plain bisect with a few retries is enough and costs less. Where it fails rarely, the number of retries has to be guessed before the rate is known, and guessing low gives a confident wrong answer. The statistical bisect spent more there, 168 replays each, and did not name anyone until it was sure. `eval/sealed/README.md` has the table and `eval/sealed/plain/` has the records.
258	
259	The second measurement: `whole-history` was run again without the entire-graph alibis and without traffic. It took 30 replays across 8 commits to reach 95.4%, against 20 replays across 5 commits and 99.8% with them. One run each way.
260	
261	Other things since the last entry: a casebook page at `cases/index.html` lists every case, `whodunit investigate --fresh` starts a case over for the video, queries to neatroots now page past its 200-row limit, and the fast tests run in a GitHub Actions workflow. The onset from traffic alone is not sharp on this history: with five regressions in it and only "errored or flagged" to go on, it brackets the whole range. The per-case witness, which judges each run against what the case expects, is what the headline run used.

2	
3	import hashlib
4	import os
5	import signal
6	import subprocess
7	import threading
8	import time
9	from collections import defaultdict
10	from dataclasses import dataclass
11	from pathlib import Path

13	from .case import Case, CaseInput, judge
14	from .suspects import git, resolve
15	
16	PASS, FAIL, SKIP = "pass", "fail", "skip"
17	
18	
19	@dataclass(frozen=True)
20	class Replay:
21	    sha: str
22	    input: str
23	    verdict: str  # pass, fail or skip
24	    reason: str
25	    seconds: float
26	    started: float = 0.0  # wall clock, seconds since the epoch
27	    tag: str = ""  # the case tag this replay's run carries in its trace, unique to the replay
28	
29	
30	def run_command(command: list[str], cwd: Path, env: dict, timeout: float) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
31	    """Like subprocess.run, but a timeout stops the whole process group.
32	
33	    The replay command is usually `uv run ...`, which starts the agent as a child. Killing only
34	    `uv` would leave the agent running.
35	    """
36	    process = subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=env, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, start_new_session=True)
37	    try:
38	        stdout, stderr = process.communicate(timeout=timeout)
39	    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
40	        try:
41	            os.killpg(process.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
42	        except ProcessLookupError:
43	            pass
44	        process.communicate()
45	        raise
46	    return subprocess.CompletedProcess(command, process.returncode, stdout, stderr)
47	
48	
49	class Runner:
50	    """Keeps one worktree per commit under .whodunit/worktrees and counts every replay it runs."""
51	
52	    def __init__(self, repo: str | Path, case: Case, keep: bool = False):
53	        self.repo = Path(repo).resolve()
54	        self.case = case
55	        self.keep = keep
56	        # One folder per runner, so two runs in the same repo never remove each other's worktrees.
57	        self.root = self.repo / ".whodunit" / "worktrees" / str(os.getpid())
58	        self.built: dict[str, str | None] = {}  # sha -> None if the build worked, else why it did not
59	        self.replays: list[Replay] = []
60	        self._locks: dict[str, threading.Lock] = defaultdict(threading.Lock)  # one build at a time per commit
61	        self._turn: dict[str, int] = defaultdict(int)  # which input a commit gets next
62	        self._count = 0
63	        self._first = int(time.time()) % 100000 * 1000  # so tags from separate runs of one case never collide
64	        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(self.repo), "worktree", "prune"], capture_output=True)
65	
66	    def __enter__(self):
67	        return self
68	
69	    def __exit__(self, *exc):
70	        if not self.keep:
71	            self.clean()
72	
73	    def worktree(self, sha: str) -> Path:
74	        path = self.root / sha[:12]
75	        if not path.exists():
76	            self.root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
77	            git(self.repo, "worktree", "add", "--detach", "--force", str(path), sha)
78	        return path
79	
80	    def clean(self) -> None:
81	        for sha in list(self.built):
82	            path = self.root / sha[:12]
83	            if path.exists():
84	                subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(self.repo), "worktree", "remove", "--force", str(path)], capture_output=True)
85	        self.built.clear()
86	        try:
87	            self.root.rmdir()
88	        except OSError:
89	            pass
90	
91	    def _env(self, sha: str, tag: str = "") -> dict:
92	        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if k != "VIRTUAL_ENV"}
93	        env.update(self.case.env)
94	        env["WHODUNIT_COMMIT"] = sha
95	        if self.case.id:
96	            env["WHODUNIT_CASE"] = tag or self.case.id
97	        else:
98	            env.pop("WHODUNIT_CASE", None)  # ordinary traffic carries no case tag
99	        lock = self.root / sha[:12] / self.case.target / "uv.lock"
100	        if lock.is_file():
101	            # Worktrees with the same lockfile share one environment, so a new commit does not
102	            # mean a new install. A commit that changes the lockfile gets its own.
103	            digest = hashlib.sha256(lock.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:12]
104	            env.setdefault("UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT", str(self.repo / ".whodunit" / "envs" / digest))
105	        dotenv = self.repo / ".env"
106	        if dotenv.is_file():
107	            env.setdefault("WHODUNIT_ENV", str(dotenv))  # a path only; the agent reads the keys itself
108	        return env
109	
110	    def build(self, sha: str) -> str | None:
111	        """Check the commit out and build it once. Returns why it failed, or None."""
112	        with self._locks[sha]:
113	            return self._build(sha)
114	
115	    def _build(self, sha: str) -> str | None:
116	        if sha in self.built:
117	            return self.built[sha]
118	        problem = None
119	        cwd = self.worktree(sha) / self.case.target
120	        if not cwd.is_dir():
121	            problem = f"{self.case.target} does not exist at this commit"
122	        elif self.case.build:
123	            try:
124	                done = run_command(list(self.case.build), cwd, self._env(sha), self.case.timeout)
125	                if done.returncode != 0:
126	                    problem = "build failed: " + ((done.stderr.strip() or done.stdout.strip()).splitlines() or ["no output"])[-1]
127	            except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired) as exc:
128	                problem = f"build failed: {exc}"
129	        self.built[sha] = problem
130	        return problem
131	
132	    def replay(self, ref: str, case_input: CaseInput) -> Replay:
133	        """Run the agent once at this commit with this input and judge the result."""
134	        sha = resolve(self.repo, ref)
135	        started, clock = time.monotonic(), time.time()
136	        with self._locks["#"]:
137	            self._count += 1
138	            # The agent writes WHODUNIT_CASE into its trace, so a number after the case id lets
139	            # one replay be matched to exactly one run afterwards.
140	            tag = f"{self.case.id}/{self._first + self._count}" if self.case.id else ""
141	        problem = self.build(sha)
142	        if problem:
143	            verdict, reason = SKIP, problem
144	        else:
145	            cwd = self.worktree(sha) / self.case.target
146	            command = [part.replace("{input}", case_input.text) for part in self.case.run]
147	            try:
148	                done = run_command(command, cwd, self._env(sha, tag), self.case.timeout)
149	                passed, reason = judge(self.case, case_input, done.stdout, cwd)
150	                if not passed and done.returncode != 0:
151	                    reason = f"exit {done.returncode}: " + ((done.stderr.strip().splitlines() or [reason])[-1])
152	                verdict = PASS if passed else FAIL
153	            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
154	                verdict, reason = FAIL, f"timed out after {self.case.timeout:.0f}s"
155	        result = Replay(sha=sha, input=case_input.text, verdict=verdict, reason=reason, seconds=time.monotonic() - started, started=clock, tag=tag)
156	        self.replays.append(result)
157	        return result
158	
159	    def test_commit(self, ref: str) -> tuple[str, list[Replay]]:
160	        """Every input once. The commit fails if any input fails, and is skipped if it will not build."""
161	        results = []
162	        for case_input in self.case.inputs:
163	            result = self.replay(ref, case_input)
164	            results.append(result)
165	            if result.verdict != PASS:
166	                return result.verdict, results
167	        return PASS, results
168	
169	    def trial(self, ref: str) -> str:
170	        """One replay at this commit, taking the case inputs in turn. This is what the statistical bisect calls."""
171	        sha = resolve(self.repo, ref)
172	        with self._locks[sha]:
173	            turn = self._turn[sha]
174	            self._turn[sha] += 1
175	        return self.replay(sha, self.case.inputs[turn % len(self.case.inputs)]).verdict

    26	def plain_bisect(count: int, test: Callable[[int], str]) -> Lineup:
    27	    """Find the first failing suspect among `count`, oldest first.
    28	
    29	    The commit before suspect 0 is known good and the last suspect is known bad. `test(i)` returns
    30	    pass, fail or skip. A skipped commit cannot be judged, so the search steps to its nearest
    31	    untested neighbour, as `git bisect skip` does. If only skipped commits separate the last
    32	    pass from the first fail, they all stay in `remaining`.
    33	    """
    34	    if count < 1:
    35	        raise ValueError("there are no suspects")
    36	    good, bad = -1, count - 1  # the first bad commit is in (good, bad]
    37	    skipped: set[int] = set()
    38	    tested: list[tuple[int, str]] = []
    39	    while True:
    40	        open_ = [i for i in range(good + 1, bad) if i not in skipped]
    41	        if not open_:
    42	            break
    43	        middle = (good + bad) / 2
    44	        pick = min(open_, key=lambda i: (abs(i - middle), i))
    45	        verdict = test(pick)
    46	        tested.append((pick, verdict))
    47	        if verdict == PASS:
    48	            good = pick
    49	        elif verdict == FAIL:
    50	            bad = pick
    51	        else:
    52	            skipped.add(pick)
    53	    remaining = list(range(good + 1, bad + 1))
    54	    return Lineup(culprit=bad if len(remaining) == 1 else None, remaining=remaining, tested=tested)

172	    for block in answer.split("\n=== end"):
173	        head, _, body = block.partition("=== ")[2].partition("\n")
174	        name = head.strip()
175	        if not name:
176	            continue
177	        if name not in allowed:
178	            problems.append(f"{name} is not one of the files the culprit touched")
179	            continue
180	        text = original = (worktree / name).read_text()
181	        edits = EDIT.findall(body)
182	        if not edits and body.strip() and "<<<<<<<" not in body:
183	            text = body.rstrip("\n") + "\n"  # a whole file, which is also accepted
184	        for search, replace in edits:
185	            if text.count(search) != 1:
186	                problems.append(f"an edit to {name} matched {text.count(search)} places and needs to match exactly one")
187	                continue
188	            text = text.replace(search, replace)
189	        if text != original:
190	            (worktree / name).write_text(text)
191	            changed.append(name)
192	    return changed, "; ".join(problems)

195	def patch(repo: str | Path, culprit: str, base: str, case_id: str, target: str, request: str | None, brief: dict | None, feedback: str = "") -> Fix:
196	    """Ask a model for a patch that keeps the culprit's intent, and commit it on a new branch."""
197	    repo = Path(repo).resolve()
198	    branch = f"whodunit/{case_id}"
199	    worktree = fix_worktree(repo, branch, base)
200	    subject = git(repo, "show", "-s", "--format=%s", culprit).strip()
201	    files = [f for f in git(repo, "diff-tree", "--no-commit-id", "--name-only", "-r", culprit, "--", target).split("\n") if f and (worktree / f).is_file()]
202	    if not files:
203	        return Fix(branch, "patch", note="None of the files the culprit touched exist at the bad ref.")
204	    parts = [
205	        f"Request behind the culprit commit: {request or 'not recorded'}",
206	        f"Culprit commit {culprit[:12]}: {subject}",
207	        "Its diff:\n" + git(repo, "show", "--format=", culprit, "--", target)[:6000],
208	        "Root-cause brief:\n" + "\n".join(s["text"] for s in (brief or {}).get("sentences", [])),
209	    ]
210	    if feedback:
211	        parts.append("An earlier patch was tried and the failure is still there. What happened:\n" + feedback)
212	    parts += [f"Current content of {f}:\n{(worktree / f).read_text()}" for f in files]
213	    try:
214	        answer = llm.ask(PATCH_SYSTEM, "\n\n".join(parts), max_tokens=3000, timeout=300)
215	    except llm.LlmError as exc:
216	        return Fix(branch, "patch", note=f"No patch was written: {exc}")
217	    changed, problems = apply_edits(answer, worktree, files)
218	    if not changed or not git(worktree, "status", "--porcelain").strip():
219	        return Fix(branch, "patch", note="The model's answer changed none of the culprit's files." + (f" {problems}." if problems else ""))
220	    sha = _commit(worktree, f"Patch the regression from \"{subject}\"\n\nWhodunit case {case_id} named {culprit[:12]}. This keeps what that commit was for and removes the failure.")
221	    return Fix(branch, "patch", sha, files=changed)

1	"""The motive: what was the culprit commit asked to do?
2	
3	Entire keeps a checkpoint for a commit that followed coding-agent work, with the session
4	transcript behind it. This module finds the request that led to the commit and the part of
5	the session where the agent worked on it.
6	"""
7	
8	import json
9	import re
10	import subprocess
11	from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
12	from datetime import datetime, timezone
13	from pathlib import Path
14	
15	from .suspects import git
16	
17	MAX_TEXT = 1200  # characters kept from any one transcript entry
18	
19	
20	@dataclass
21	class Step:
22	    """One thing the coding agent said or did between the request and the commit."""
23	
24	    id: str  # transcript entry id, shortened, so a brief can cite it
25	    kind: str  # said, edited, ran or read
26	    text: str
27	    file: str | None = None
28	
29	
30	@dataclass
31	class Motive:
32	    sha: str
33	    subject: str
34	    checkpoint: str | None = None
35	    session: str | None = None
36	    agent: str | None = None
37	    model: str | None = None
38	    request: str | None = None  # the prompt that led to the commit
39	    message: str = ""  # the commit message body, which is all there is when no session can be read
40	    request_id: str | None = None
41	    request_time: str | None = None
42	    earlier_requests: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # prompts before it in the same session, oldest first
43	    steps: list[Step] = field(default_factory=list)
44	    link: str | None = None
45	    note: str = ""  # why something is missing
46	
47	    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
48	        return asdict(self)
49	
50	
51	def entire(repo: str | Path, *args: str) -> str | None:
52	    """Run the Entire CLI. Returns None if it is not installed or the call fails."""
53	    try:
54	        done = subprocess.run(["entire", *args], cwd=repo, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=120)
55	    except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
56	        return None
57	    return done.stdout if done.returncode == 0 else None

60	def checkpoint_link(repo: str | Path, sha: str) -> str | None:
61	    """https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/FULL_SHA, if the repo has a GitHub remote."""
62	    try:
63	        url = git(repo, "remote", "get-url", "origin").strip()
64	    except RuntimeError:
65	        return None
66	    match = re.search(r"github\.com[:/]([^/]+)/([^/]+?)(?:\.git)?$", url)
67	    return f"https://entire.io/gh/{match.group(1)}/{match.group(2)}/commit/{sha}" if match else None
68	
69	
70	def _when(stamp: str | None) -> datetime | None:
71	    if not stamp:
72	        return None
73	    try:
74	        return datetime.fromisoformat(stamp.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
75	    except ValueError:
76	        return None

79	def _prompt_text(entry: dict) -> str | None:
80	    """The text of a prompt a person typed, or None for tool results and injected context."""
81	    if entry.get("type") != "user" or entry.get("isMeta") or entry.get("isSidechain"):
82	        return None
83	    content = entry.get("message", {}).get("content")
84	    if isinstance(content, str):
85	        return content.strip() or None
86	    if isinstance(content, list) and not any(b.get("type") == "tool_result" for b in content):
87	        text = "\n".join(b.get("text", "") for b in content if b.get("type") == "text").strip()
88	        return text or None
89	    return None
90	
91	
92	def _steps(entry: dict, files: set[str]) -> list[Step]:
93	    """What an assistant entry said and did. Edits and reads are kept only for files in the commit."""
94	    out = []
95	    entry_id = (entry.get("uuid") or "")[:8]
96	    for block in entry.get("message", {}).get("content", []) or []:
97	        if block.get("type") == "text" and block.get("text", "").strip():
98	            out.append(Step(entry_id, "said", block["text"].strip()[:MAX_TEXT]))
99	        elif block.get("type") == "tool_use":
100	            name, given = block.get("name", ""), block.get("input", {}) or {}
101	            path = given.get("file_path") or ""
102	            touched = next((f for f in files if path.endswith(f)), None)
103	            if name in ("Edit", "Write", "NotebookEdit") and touched:
104	                change = given.get("new_string") or given.get("content") or ""
105	                out.append(Step(entry_id, "edited", change[:MAX_TEXT], touched))
106	            elif name == "Read" and touched:
107	                out.append(Step(entry_id, "read", touched, touched))
108	            elif name == "Bash" and (given.get("description") or given.get("command")):
109	                out.append(Step(entry_id, "ran", (given.get("description") or given["command"])[:300]))
110	    return out

113	def read_transcript(entries: list[dict], commit_time: datetime, files: set[str], max_steps: int = 40) -> dict:
114	    """Find the request behind a commit made at `commit_time`, and what the agent did about it.
115	
116	    The request is the last prompt a person typed before the commit. A checkpoint can cover
117	    several commits from one long turn, so the commit time is what ties a prompt to a commit.
118	    """
119	    prompts = []
120	    for entry in entries:
121	        text, at = _prompt_text(entry), _when(entry.get("timestamp"))
122	        if text and at and at <= commit_time:
123	            prompts.append((at, text, (entry.get("uuid") or "")[:8]))
124	    if not prompts:
125	        return {"request": None, "earlier_requests": [], "steps": []}
126	    asked_at, request, request_id = prompts[-1]
127	    steps = []
128	    for entry in entries:
129	        at = _when(entry.get("timestamp"))
130	        if entry.get("type") == "assistant" and not entry.get("isSidechain") and at and asked_at <= at <= commit_time:
131	            steps += _steps(entry, files)
132	    # Keep everything that touched the commit's files, and fill the rest with what was said most recently.
133	    keep = [s for s in steps if s.file][-max_steps:]
134	    rest = [s for s in steps if not s.file][-max(0, max_steps - len(keep)):]
135	    order = {id(s): n for n, s in enumerate(steps)}
136	    chosen = sorted(keep + rest, key=lambda s: order[id(s)])
137	    return {
138	        "request": request, "request_id": request_id, "request_time": asked_at.isoformat(),
139	        "earlier_requests": [text for _, text, _ in prompts[:-1]][-5:], "steps": chosen,
140	    }
141

143	def find_motive(repo: str | Path, sha: str) -> Motive:
144	    """Everything Entire knows about why this commit was made."""
145	    full, subject, stamp, trailer = git(
146	        repo, "show", "-s", "--format=%H%x00%s%x00%cI%x00%(trailers:key=Entire-Checkpoint,valueonly,separator=%x20)", sha
147	    ).strip().split("\x00")
148	    body = git(repo, "show", "-s", "--format=%b", full)
149	    body = "\n".join(line for line in body.splitlines() if not re.match(r"^[A-Za-z-]+: ", line)).strip()  # drop trailers
150	    motive = Motive(sha=full, subject=subject, link=checkpoint_link(repo, full), message=body)
151	    if not trailer.strip():
152	        motive.note = "This commit has no Entire checkpoint, so there is no recorded request behind it."
153	        return motive
154	    motive.checkpoint = trailer.split()[0]
155	    meta = entire(repo, "checkpoint", "explain", "--checkpoint", motive.checkpoint, "--json")
156	    if meta is None:
157	        motive.note = f"The commit names Entire checkpoint {motive.checkpoint}, and Entire cannot find it, so the request behind this commit is not on record."
158	        return motive
159	    sessions = json.loads(meta).get("sessions") or [{}]
160	    files = {f for f in git(repo, "diff-tree", "--no-commit-id", "--name-only", "-r", full).split("\n") if f}
161	    made_at = datetime.fromisoformat(stamp).astimezone(timezone.utc)
162	    # A checkpoint takes in every session that was open in the folder when the commit was made,
163	    # including ones that had nothing to do with it. The session wanted is the one that edited
164	    # the commit's files.
165	    best, best_score, chosen = None, -1.0, 0
166	    for index in range(len(sessions)):
167	        raw = entire(repo, "checkpoint", "explain", "--checkpoint", motive.checkpoint, "--session-index", str(index), "--raw-transcript")
168	        if not raw:
169	            continue
170	        entries = []
171	        for line in raw.splitlines():
172	            try:
173	                entries.append(json.loads(line))
174	            except json.JSONDecodeError:
175	                continue
176	        candidate = read_transcript(entries, made_at, files)
177	        if candidate["request"] is None:
178	            continue
179	        score = sum(1.0 for step in candidate["steps"] if step.kind == "edited") + (0.5 if any(step.kind == "ran" and "ommit" in step.text for step in candidate["steps"]) else 0.0)
180	        if score > best_score:
181	            best, best_score, chosen = candidate, score, index
182	    if best is None:
183	        motive.note = "The checkpoint has no transcript with a prompt from before this commit."
184	        return motive
185	    found = best
186	    motive.session, motive.agent, motive.model = (sessions[chosen].get(k) for k in ("session_id", "agent", "model"))
187	    if len(sessions) > 1:
188	        motive.note = (f"This checkpoint holds {len(sessions)} sessions. " + (
189	            "The one that edited the commit's files was used." if best_score >= 1 else "None of them edited the commit's files, so the request shown may not be the cause of this commit."))
190	    for key, value in found.items():
191	        setattr(motive, key, value)
192	    # A session transcript is full of absolute paths. The case file is public, so they go.
193	    here, home = str(Path(repo).resolve()), str(Path.home())
194	
195	    def scrub(text: str) -> str:
196	        return text.replace(here + "/", "").replace(here, ".").replace(home, "~")
197	
198	    motive.request = scrub(motive.request)
199	    motive.earlier_requests = [scrub(t) for t in motive.earlier_requests]
200	    for step in motive.steps:
201	        step.text = scrub(step.text)
202	    return motive

    54	def find_onset(workflow: str, runs: list[dict], floor: float = 0.01) -> Onset:
    55	    """Where the failures begin, given runs as {"commit", "started_ms", "bad", "input_preview"}, oldest first.
    56	
    57	    Commits are ordered by when they were first seen. The oldest commit is taken as the baseline.
    58	    The good ref is the last commit before the change point's posterior reaches `floor`, so the
    59	    range handed to the lineup is wide enough to hold the culprit.
    60	    """
    61	    order: dict[str, dict] = {}
    62	    for run in runs:
    63	        seen = order.setdefault(run["commit"], {"sha": run["commit"], "first_seen_ms": run["started_ms"], "runs": 0, "bad": 0})
    64	        seen["runs"] += 1
    65	        seen["bad"] += run["bad"]
    66	    commits = list(order.values())
    67	    onset = Onset(workflow=workflow, commits=commits, runs=len(runs), bad_runs=sum(r["bad"] for r in runs))
    68	    if len(commits) < 2:
    69	        onset.note = "Runs from at least two commits are needed to place the onset."
    70	        return onset
    71	    if onset.bad_runs == 0:
    72	        onset.note = "No bad runs in the traffic."
    73	        return onset
    74	    state = ChangePoint(len(commits) - 1)  # the oldest commit plays the good ref
    75	    for position, commit in enumerate(commits):
    76	        for _ in range(commit["bad"]):
    77	            state.observe(position - 1, True)
    78	        for _ in range(commit["runs"] - commit["bad"]):
    79	            state.observe(position - 1, False)

    81	    top = max(range(len(posterior)), key=posterior.__getitem__)

    84	        mass += share

    89	    onset.bad = commits[-1]["sha"]

     1	# Whodunit
     2	
     3	41 commits since it last worked. Which one did it?
     4	
     5	Whodunit answers two questions about an AI agent that used to work and now fails: which commit broke it, and why that commit was made. Then it fixes the commit, proves the fix by replaying the failures, and counts what the breakage cost.
     6	
     7	It was built for neatHack between 10 and 12 October 2026. `hackathon.md` is the dated build log, including the parts that went wrong.
     8	
     9	## Why plain bisect is not enough
    10	
    11	`git bisect` assumes a bad commit fails every time. Agents do not behave that way. A prompt change might break one run in three, and a commit that is perfectly fine might still fail one run in twenty. Test a bad commit once, see it pass, and bisect walks off in the wrong direction without telling you.
    12	
    13	Whodunit replays the failing inputs against suspect commits and keeps a probability for each suspect being the first bad one. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure. If the replay budget runs out first, it hands back the suspects still in the lineup with their probabilities.
    14	
    15	How well that works is measured two ways. [eval/sealed](eval/sealed/README.md) is five regressions planted by a separate session with a sealed answer key: three were named inside 120 replays, all five after more, and no commit was wrongly accused. Plain bisect with five retries, on the same five, got three right with fewer replays, named an innocent commit on the fourth and could not start on the fifth. [eval/simulator](eval/simulator/README.md) is simulated cases with a known culprit. The short version: when good commits never fail, plain bisect with repeats is cheaper. When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own, it falls apart and the statistical bisect does not.
    16	
    17	## How a case runs
    18	
    19	A case is a small TOML file: a symptom, the failing inputs with what each should have produced, the last good ref and the first bad ref. One command runs all of it:
    20	
    21	```bash
    22	uv run whodunit investigate cases/whole-history.toml --from-traffic refund-agent
    23	```
    24	
    25	It stops only when it needs the owner's ruling. Each step is also a command of its own (`lineup`, `brief`, `ruling`, `fix`, `damages`, `open-case`), and each adds to one record next to the case file. The case file page is drawn from that record.
    26	
    27	On the refund agent's real history, 57 commits grown by a separate coding session, that command named the culprit at 99.8% after 20 replays, quoted the request that caused it, patched it, proved the patch on 30 clean replays and counted 120.00 in refunds that had gone to the wrong people. [evidence/casefile-whole-history.png](evidence/casefile-whole-history.png) is the page it wrote.
    28	
    29	0. Before any replay, two things narrow the field. entire-graph says which commits could not have reached the agent (a README edit, a helper script the agent never calls), and those start with less suspicion. And ordinary runs that already asked what the case asks are evidence that is already paid for.
    30	1. The lineup checks every suspect commit out into its own git worktree and replays the case inputs there. Each replay is a real run of the agent, traced to neatroots and tagged with the commit and the case. A commit that will not build is skipped, as `git bisect skip` does.
    31	2. The motive comes from Entire. A commit made by a coding agent carries a checkpoint, and the checkpoint holds the session. Whodunit finds the prompt that led to the commit and what the coding agent did next.
    32	3. The brief is written by a model from the culprit's diff, that slice of the session, and a failing run set against a passing one. Every sentence has to cite a span, a commit or a checkpoint that is really in the evidence. Sentences that do not are cut.
    33	4. The ruling is the owner's. It is asked once per kind of change (a prompt change, a tool change, a dependency) and remembered under `rulings/`.
    34	5. The fix is a revert or a patch on a local branch. It is proven only when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%, which takes about 30 clean replays. A patch that is not proven is tried once more with its failures in view, and after that the culprit is reverted. The case is kept under `cases/` as a regression test that `whodunit check` can replay against any ref.
    35	6. The damages are counted from the traces: how many runs went bad since the culprit, what they cost in tokens, and what they cost the shop, read from the refund tool's spans.
    36	
    37	Whodunit never pushes, opens a pull request or writes to anyone's finance model by itself. Those stay with the owner.
    38	
    39	## Try it
    40	
    41	You need Python 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), git and a running neatroots.
    42	
    43	```bash
    44	uv sync
    45	uv run pytest -m "not slow"                    # the fast tests, no model and no keys
    46	
    47	# A throwaway repo with 20 commits, the refund agent and a planted bug:
    48	uv run python tests/planted.py /tmp/planted
    49	uv run python victims/refund-agent/fake_llm.py &
    50	uv run whodunit lineup /tmp/planted/case.toml --repo /tmp/planted --method plain
    51	```
    52	
    53	Add `flaky-lookup 40 27` to the `planted.py` line for 40 commits with a bug at commit 27 that fails about one run in three, and drop `--method plain` to use the statistical bisect.
    54	
    55	`uv run python -m whodunit.simulate --out eval/simulator` regenerates the simulator charts, and `uv run whodunit casebook` rewrites every case file and the index at `cases/index.html`.
    56	
    57	## What is in here
    58	
    59	- `whodunit/` is the tool. `lineup.py` holds both bisects, `replay.py` the worktree runner, `motive.py` the Entire lookups, `brief.py` the evidence and the brief, `ruling.py`, `fix.py` and `damages.py` the closing steps, and `casefile/` the page.
    60	- `victims/refund-agent/` is the agent under investigation. It started as the `refund-agent` example that ships with neatroots, which is licensed under Apache-2.0. The licence is in that folder and the changes are listed in its README.
    61	- `eval/simulator/` has the accuracy curves, the tables behind them and what they show.
    62	- `tests/planted.py` builds histories with a known culprit. The tests and the demo use the same builder.
    63	- `AGENTS.md` is the working brief for anyone writing code here.
    64	
    65	## Models and keys
    66	
    67	Keys live in `.env`, which git ignores. `.env.example` lists them. The code that needs a key reads the file itself.
    68	
    69	Replays of the refund agent use a scripted model by default and cost nothing. `REFUND_LLM=gateway` or `REFUND_LLM=own` switches them to a real model. Keep one model for the whole of a case, because a model change in the middle would look like a regression.
    70	
    71	The brief and the patch use `WHODUNIT_LLM`: `gateway`, `own`, `agent` for a coding agent in headless mode, or `none` for a fixed template with no model.
    72	
    73	## What it does not do yet
    74	
    75	- The statistical bisect assumes one change point. Two regressions in the same range will confuse it.
    76	- A replay that times out counts as a failure, so a badly overloaded machine can frame an innocent commit.
    77	- Damages are estimates from token counts and list prices.

     1	# Simulator results
     2	
     3	How often does the lineup name the right commit, for a given number of replays? This folder answers that with simulated cases, where the culprit is known.
     4	
     5	Each case has 40 suspect commits and one culprit picked at random. Every point is 500 cases. Three methods get the same cases and the same replay budget:
     6	
     7	- The statistical bisect in `whodunit/lineup.py`. It names a commit only when it is 95% sure, and otherwise hands back the suspects that remain with their probabilities.
     8	- Plain bisect with repeats. It replays each commit as many times as the budget allows and calls the commit bad on the first failure.
     9	- Plain bisect with one replay per commit, which is what `git bisect run` does.
    10	
    11	To regenerate everything here, run `uv run python -m whodunit.simulate --out eval/simulator`. It takes about two minutes. `tables.md` has every number behind the charts, and `results.json` has the raw counts.
    12	
    13	## When good commits never fail
    14	
    15	![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits never fail](accuracy-clean-baseline.svg)
    16	
    17	Plain bisect with repeats wins here at every budget. For a bug that fails 30% of the time, 80 replays get it to 97% while the statistical bisect names the right commit in 67% of cases. The statistical bisect needs 160 replays to reach 93%.
    18	
    19	The reason is that plain bisect with repeats assumes a single failure convicts a commit, and in this world that is true. The statistical bisect does not assume it. It starts out believing a good commit fails about 5% of the time and spends replays finding out.
    20	
    21	Two things are worth knowing before picking plain bisect on that basis. Its mistakes are silent: with 40 replays on the 30% bug it names the wrong commit in 26% of cases and gives no sign of it, where the statistical bisect names the wrong one in 2% and says "not sure yet" in the rest. And the dashed line shows the statistical bisect's top suspect is right in 91% of cases at 80 replays, so most of its "not sure yet" answers are pointing at the culprit already.
    22	
    23	Plain bisect with one replay per commit is right 10% of the time on the 30% bug, at any budget.
    24	
    25	## When good commits fail 5% of the time on their own
    26	
    27	![Accuracy against replay budget when good commits fail 5% of the time](accuracy-flaky-baseline.svg)
    28	
    29	Agents are rarely this clean. Give every good commit a 5% chance of failing by itself and plain bisect with repeats falls apart, and more replays make it worse. On the 30% bug it is right in 31% of cases with 40 replays and 4% with 320, because every extra replay of an innocent commit is another chance for a stray failure to convict it. Even a bug that fails every time is found in only 46% of cases at 40 replays.
    30	
    31	The statistical bisect holds up. On the 30% bug it names the right commit in 60% of cases with 160 replays and 84% with 320. On a bug that fails every time it is right in 99% of cases and uses about 21 replays.
    32	
    33	## Where it falls short
    34	
    35	- A bug that fails 20% of the time on a flaky baseline is named in only 46% of cases, even with 320 replays. The top suspect is right in 70%.
    36	- The 95% bar is not always met. Across the cells, the share of cases with a wrong accusation runs from 0% to 7%, and the 7% is the 30% bug on a flaky baseline at 320 replays. The model assumes one change point and two fixed failure rates, and the prior on the good rate is a guess.
    37	- These are simulated commits with independent replays. Real replays share a model provider and a machine, so their failures can come in bursts, which this does not capture.
    38	- Small budgets are spent mostly on warming up. Below about 30 replays the statistical bisect rarely names anyone unless the bug fails every time.
    39	
    40	## What changed from the first design
    41	
    42	Two things, both found by simulating the 30% bug across 40 suspects with 300 replays allowed.
    43	
    44	The first version put a uniform prior on both failure rates, so it had to learn from scratch that good commits mostly pass. It solved 59% of cases. Starting from the belief that a good commit fails about 5% of the time, loosely held, took that to 93%.
    45	
    46	The brief said to test the commit that splits the posterior mass most evenly. The code now defaults to the replay with the highest expected information gain, and keeps the even split as `how="split"`. With the uniform prior the difference was large, 92% against 59%. With the current prior it is small: 282 cases solved against 280 out of 300, using 79 replays on average against 83. So the prior did the work, and the choice of picker barely matters.
---- eval/sealed/README.md
     1	# Sealed eval, 11 October 2026
     2	
     3	Five regressions were planted in the refund agent's history by a second coding session, through ordinary requests to fresh coding sessions. It wrote the answer key, and the key's SHA-256 was committed in 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case. `eval/score.py` checks the key against that hash before scoring. The key was added to git only after every case had been run.
     4	
     5	Replays ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, three at a time.
     6	
     7	## Result
     8	
     9	With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 cases where nobody was named.
    10	
    11	The two open cases were then resumed from their own replays with up to 200 more allowed: 5 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations.
    12	
    13	| Case | Rate the second session measured | Rate Whodunit estimated | At 120 replays | In the end | Replays | Commits replayed | Suspects |
    14	| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    15	| cents-off | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 21 | 5 | 13 |
    16	| wrong-order-refunded | 30% | 12% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 9 | 12 |
    17	| half-done-batch | 25% | 14% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 10 | 15 |
    18	| strangers-paid | 72% | 59% | solved | solved | 30 | 5 | 11 |
    19	| turned-away | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 24 | 6 | 14 |
    20	
    21	The rate Whodunit estimates is a posterior mean, so after only a few replays it sits below 100% even for a bug that fails every time.
    22	
    23	## What it cost
    24	
    25	Replay spend on the gateway, estimated from token counts at list prices, came to about $1.91 for all five cases:
    26	
    27	- cents-off: about $0.08 (61,267 tokens)
    28	- wrong-order-refunded: about $0.57 (438,034 tokens)
    29	- half-done-batch: about $1.04 (795,110 tokens)
    30	- strangers-paid: about $0.10 (78,530 tokens)
    31	- turned-away: about $0.12 (100,111 tokens)
    32	
    33	## What this does and does not show
    34	
    35	- No commit was wrongly accused, at either budget. On `half-done-batch` the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody. That is the behaviour the 95% bar is for.
    36	- The two cases it could not close at 120 replays are the two that fail least often. Whodunit put them at 12% and 14%, where the second session had measured 30% and 25% from a handful of probes. A bug that rare needs a lot of replays whatever the method.
    37	- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects. On ranges this size a careful scan from the oldest commit would have replayed about as many commits as Whodunit did, so this eval says little about savings on long histories. The simulator in `eval/simulator` covers 40 suspects.
    38	- Five cases is a small sample. It is enough to say the pipeline works on a history it did not write, and not enough to put a number on accuracy.
    39	- Each case has one planted regression inside its range, by design. Two regressions that touch the same inputs in one range are outside what the model assumes.
    40	
    41	## What happened after the culprits were named
    42	
    43	The owner's ruling was patch for all three kinds of change involved. A fix counts as proven when its failure rate is back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit, at 95%.
    44	
    45	| Case | Outcome | Tries | Replays of the final fix |
    46	| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
    47	| cents-off | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 30 |
    48	| strangers-paid | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 30 |
    49	| wrong-order-refunded | patched and proven | 1 | 0 failures in 36 |
    50	| turned-away | two patches not proven, then reverted and proven | 3 | 0 failures in 30 |
    51	| half-done-batch | not fixed | 3 | two patches left 5 failures in 90 each, and the revert conflicts |
    52	
    53	So four of five were closed, one of them only by giving up on the patch the owner asked for, and one was left open and says so.
    54	
    55	## The same culprit across the whole history
    56	
    57	`cases/whole-history.toml` takes the `strangers-paid` regression and widens the range to the whole grown history, 57 suspects. With alibis from entire-graph for 22 of them and 18 ordinary runs as evidence, 20 replays across 5 commits named the culprit at 99.8%. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 37 commits. This is the run that speaks to savings on a longer history, and it is one run.
    58	
    59	## Against plain bisect with retries
    60	
    61	The same five cases were then given to plain bisect, with each commit replayed up to 5 times over and called bad on the first failure. It ran once per case, so this is one sample and not a rate.
    62	
    63	| Case | Plain bisect, 5 retries | Its replays | Statistical bisect | Its replays |
    64	| --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
    65	| cents-off | right | 15 | right | 21 |
    66	| strangers-paid | right | 15 | right | 30 |
    67	| turned-away | right | 25 | right | 24 |
    68	| wrong-order-refunded | wrong commit named | 19 | right | 168 |
    69	| half-done-batch | could not start: the bad ref passed 10 replays in a row | 10 | right | 168 |
    70	
    71	On the three bugs that fail most of the time, plain bisect was right and used 55 replays in all against 75. That matches the simulator: with a clean baseline, and this one was clean (0 failures in 211 replays of commits before a culprit), plain bisect with retries is the cheaper tool.
    72	
    73	On the two bugs that fail about one run in eight, it went wrong in the two ways it can. For `wrong-order-refunded` a bad commit passed all 5 tries, the search went the wrong way, and it named an innocent commit three places from the real one, with nothing to say it was unsure. For `half-done-batch` the bad ref itself passed 10 replays in a row, so there was nothing to bisect.
    74	
    75	More retries would have fixed both, at a cost. The trouble is that the number has to be picked before the failure rate is known. The statistical bisect does not need it picked: it spent 21 to 30 replays on the frequent bugs and 168 on the rare ones, and on the rare ones it said "not sure yet" at 120 instead of naming someone.

"""Damages: only runs that fail the case's own check are this case's damage."""

import json
import sqlite3

from whodunit import damages

CULPRIT, LATER, EARLIER = "c" * 40, "d" * 40, "a" * 40
ASKED = "Hi, I'm cust_6. Could I get a refund of 30 dollars for order 2002? Thanks."


class Traces:
    """Stands in for neatroots: answers query_sql from a small SQLite database with the same two tables."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
        self.db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        self.db.execute("create table runs (trace_id, workflow, doctor, status, error_count, finding_count, started_ms, input_preview)")
        self.db.execute("create table spans (trace_id, name, span_kind, attributes, output_preview, status_code, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens)")
        self.count = 0

    def run(self, commit, asked, refunds=(), case="", status="ok", findings=0, tokens=(1000, 100)):
        self.count += 1
        trace = f"t{self.count:031d}"
        tags = f"commit:{commit}" + (f" case:{case}" if case else "")
        self.db.execute("insert into runs values (?, 'refund-agent', 0, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", (trace, status, int(status == "error"), findings, self.count * 1000.0, asked))
        self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'run_info', 'CHAIN', ?, '{}', 0, null, 0, 0)", (trace, tags))
        self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'chat', 'LLM', '', '', 0, 'claude-haiku', ?, ?)", (trace, *tokens))
        for order, amount in refunds:
            self.db.execute("insert into spans values (?, 'issue_refund', 'TOOL', '', ?, 0, null, 0, 0)", (trace, json.dumps({"order_id": order, "refunded": amount})))
        return trace

    def call(self, tool, sql):
        assert tool == "query_sql"
        return {"rows": [dict(row) for row in self.db.execute(sql)]}


def test_only_runs_that_fail_this_cases_check_are_its_damage():
    traces = Traces()
    traces.run(CULPRIT, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])  # this case's bug: someone else's order refunded
    traces.run(LATER, ASKED)  # the same request, and the agent refused, as it should
    traces.run(LATER, "Please refund order 3003 in full for customer cust_7.", refunds=[("3003", 130.0)], status="error", findings=1)  # another regression
    traces.run(LATER, "Please refund order 1001 for customer cust_9.", findings=1)  # a finding that has nothing to do with this case
    traces.run(EARLIER, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])  # before the culprit, so not in the window
    traces.run(CULPRIT, ASKED, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)], case="strangers-paid/1")  # Whodunit's own replay
    since_culprit = [CULPRIT, LATER]
    counted = damages.count(traces, "refund-agent", commits=since_culprit, case_id="strangers-paid")
    counted = damages.count_case(traces, counted, "refund-agent", since_culprit, [(ASKED, [])])
    assert counted.runs == 4 and counted.replay_runs == 1
    assert (counted.case_runs, counted.case_bad) == (2, 1)  # the two runs that errored or were flagged for other reasons are not counted
    assert (counted.wrongly_paid, counted.withheld) == (30.0, 0.0)
    assert counted.case_bad_tokens == 1100 and counted.case_bad_usd == round((1000 * 1.0 + 100 * 5.0) / 1e6, 4)
    assert not hasattr(counted, "bad_runs")  # "N of M runs went bad" lumped every regression together, and is gone


def test_money_owed_and_not_refunded_is_counted_too():
    traces = Traces()
    owed = "Hi, I'm cust_4. Please refund order 2002, I ordered the wrong item by mistake."
    traces.run(CULPRIT, owed)
    traces.run(CULPRIT, owed, refunds=[("2002", 30.0)])
    counted = damages.count_case(traces, damages.count(traces, "refund-agent", commits=[CULPRIT]), "refund-agent", [CULPRIT], [(owed, [{"order_id": "2002", "refunded": 30.0}])])
    assert (counted.case_runs, counted.case_bad, counted.withheld, counted.wrongly_paid) == (2, 1, 30.0, 0.0)
